post: "Leadership isn't just about rising in the ranks and stepping up when it's needed. It's also about stepping back, listening to people around you, and inspiring others to build themselves up." That's Bryce Herold, a high school debater from Ohio reflecting on 5 days at the Debate and Leadership Institute. Alongside Founding Forward, BRI brought rising 10th-12th graders to Valley Forge for a week of Socratic dialogue, debate workshops, and visits to Valley Forge National Historic Park and Independence Hall, culminating in a final tournament at the historic Union League of Philadelphia. The topic they debated: Whether Congress should be required to authorize deploying national security forces into states. No easy answers. That's the point. This is what civic education looks like when it's working 👇  https://bit.ly/4vScTy8  #CivicEducation  #Leadership  #DebateEducation  #Civics

President Johnson handed Grant the War Department, hoping he would hold the door open. Grant handed it back. In 1867, Andrew Johnson suspended Secretary of War Edwin Stanton and named Grant to fill the seat while Congress was out of session. Grant took it, but only to keep someone worse out. When the Senate voted to reinstate Stanton, Grant returned the office without a fight. Johnson attacked his character in public. Grant wrote back: "My honor as a soldier and integrity as a man have been violently assailed." He had chosen the law over the man who appointed him. The Monroe Doctrine wasn't written by James Monroe. John Quincy Adams drafted it, and he had spent his whole life preparing to. Paris at age ten. St. Petersburg as a teenage secretary. Minister to the Netherlands, then Prussia, then Russia. Secretary of State at 50. In 1821, he told a Fourth of July audience that America "goes not abroad, in search of monsters to destroy." 2 years later he built that principle into a presidential address that carried another man's name and shaped American foreign policy for the next 2 centuries. The man who wrote the Constitution spent months arguing that the Bill of Rights was a bad idea. James Madison called written guarantees "parchment barriers." He thought a list of protected rights would leave every unlisted right exposed. Then, on June 8, 1789, he stood up in the First Congress and asked that body to pass one anyway. What changed his mind is the part most students never hear. It involved a promise he made on the campaign trail, a letter from a friend in Paris, and 2 states still refusing to ratify. #TDiH 1798, the Sedition Act became law. The First Amendment was 7 years old. Federalists feared the Jeffersonian opposition would prove disloyal in the undeclared Quasi-War with France. Their answer: make it a federal crime to criticize the government. Every one of the 10 people convicted under the Act was a member of the opposing party. Matthew Lyon, a sitting congressman, was convicted for campaign speeches critical of Adams. He ran his reelection campaign from prison. He won. Madison and Jefferson didn't responded with constitutional argument, the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, and with elections. The Act expired in 1801. Jefferson won the presidency. He didn't renew it. One of the most teachable early tests of the First Amendment. In May 1836, Congress passed a rule that automatically tabled, without debate, any petition mentioning slavery. When former President John Quincy Adams rose to protest, the Speaker of the House refused to recognize him. "Am I gagged?" he demanded. The answer was basically yes. And Adams spent the next 8 years fighting it, introducing 1000s of anti-slavery petitions from women, free black Americans, and enslaved people, surviving a censure attempt, and reading the Declaration of Independence into the record. Every petition was tabled without debate. On December 3, 1844, the House voted to repeal the gag rule. Even Adams's southern opponents acknowledged what he had done. Virginia Representative Henry Wise called him "the arch enemy of Southern slavery that ever existed." BRI's A250 Mini Documentary tells the full story. At the Bill of Rights Institute, we believe citizenship doesn't begin at 18. The 2026 MyImpact Challenge proves it. This year, hundreds of students from 49 states and Washington, D. C. identified needs in their communities and took action through service, entrepreneurship, and volunteerism. Book drives. Business mentorship programs. Advocacy for people with invisible disabilities. A youth-led effort to bring digital literacy to seniors that has now reached more than 2,000 people in-person and over 3 million online. These are students who didn't wait for someone else to solve the problem. They saw a need, applied civic virtues like responsibility, humility, and justice, and built something real.
